newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss puzzle over rise in big denomination notes.
newsitem.headline: Swiss puzzle over rise in big denomination notes.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) and private economists are puzzled by a rise in notes in circulation, which is causing the monetary base to expand.

SNB chief economist Georg Rich said on Monday the SNB was not being as expansive as growth in its monetary base would suggest. He said the expansion in the basic central bank money supply was due mainly to a rise in notes in circulation.
"The demand for central bank money, especially bank notes in high denominations, has risen much more strongly than expected," Rich said.
Speaking with journalists, he said he could give no single precise reason for the rise in big-denomination notes.
Martin Jetzer, chief economist at Guyerzeller Bank, said that in past decades Switzerland had seen similar periods when notes in circulation had jumped.

"There are various theories which might explain a sudden jump in big denomination notes. It could be an indication of flight capital coming into the country, but for some reason, the owner is reluctant to open a bank account," Jetzer said.
It may also reflect a traditional reaction among tax-shy Swiss investors to hold cash due to the extremely low level of Swiss interest rates. "There might be some hoarding," he said.

According to some theories, countries with a large black market labour force also see large volumes of notes in circulation, but the Swiss rise has been relatively recent and thus may not reflect this phenomenon.
Economists also note strong demand for "hard currency" cash such as German marks in Eastern European countries, and some speculate this may be a factor for Swiss francs, too.
Rich also said the distortion due to the increase in notes made the SNB's policy appear more expansive than it really was.
Rich said other money aggregates did not point to an overly expansive monetary policy.

"At the moment (monetary base growth) is clearly above the medium-term target path," Rich said. "But our monetary policy is not as expansive -- I would like to stress this -- as would appear from the massive overshooting of the target path."

The SNB's monetary base has been growing above target for the past 18 months. The SNB has tolerated an overshooting of its target during a period of prolonged economic weakness, which has been exacerbated by a strong Swiss franc.
Notes in circulation comprise the bulk of the monetary base. Bank balances held at the central bank make up the rest.
SNB data for the 10-day period to end-May showed notes in circulation at 29.3 billion Swiss francs. Sight deposits, the other component of the monetary base, were only 3.8 billion.
The SNB has set a five-year medium-term growth path for growth in its monetary base of one percent, on average, per year as compatible with long-term, non-inflationary growth.
